passage: At the bus stop outside school in Izmir, Selin asked Nour how the funeral had gone. Nour zipped her coat up to her chin. "It was a stroke," she said. "Ischaemic, left hemisphere. About four in five strokes are that kind. Dede was seventy-nine, so statistically his risk was already high." Her voice was level, like someone reading from a textbook. Selin waited. "They said the ambulance came quickly," Nour went on. "They did everything in the right order. Nobody made a mistake." The bus came. Nour found them two seats and talked about the brain's blood supply until their stop. Selin nodded and didn't argue. That night, a message lit up Selin's phone on her desk: "Dede used to peel oranges for me in one long spiral." A minute later came another: "I can't stop crying." Selin called her straight away.

qa.a: A stroke, ischaemic, in the left hemisphere.

qa.a: Nour is grieving and overwhelmed, and orderly facts keep the loss at a distance so she can speak without her voice breaking; the message about the oranges shows the sadness was there all along.

qa.q: Which choice of Selin's helped most, and why?
qa.a: Not arguing with the facts on the bus and then calling straight away when the messages came, so Nour wasn't alone when the tears finally arrived.

qa.q: What was the bus ride like for Selin, listening to the facts?
qa.a: Selin was probably unsure how to help, since a question about the funeral got a lecture back, but she chose to stay close and wait.

In the school library, Sabina had three printouts spread across the table: kidney function, dialysis, survival rates for people over seventy. Bhupen sat down with his maths book. "Aren't you on leave this week?"
"Came back early." She tapped a chart. "Nani's creatinine was rising for two years. It's a waste product. When the kidneys fail, it builds up." Her voice was the one she used for quiz club.
"Sabina, I'm really sorry about your Nani."
"Thanks. Did you know most people on dialysis in that age group..." She found the line with her finger and read it out, flat and exact.
Bhupen didn't know what to say, so he stayed. At the bell, she stacked the pages neatly. At the gate, she opened her bag and saw Nani's old blue umbrella folded inside. She stood very still, and her eyes filled. Bhupen waited beside her until her father's scooter pulled up.

qa.q: What were Sabina's three printouts about?
qa.a: Kidney function, dialysis, and survival rates for people over seventy.

qa.q: Why does Sabina seem to feel safer talking about creatinine than about her Nani?
qa.a: Explaining the illness keeps the loss at arm's length and uses her steady quiz-club voice; the grief only breaks through when she sees Nani's umbrella.

qa.q: Which choice of Bhupen's helped most, and why?
qa.a: Staying beside her without pushing, so she wasn't alone when the umbrella finally brought the sadness through.

qa.q: How might Sabina's quiz-club tone come across to classmates who don't know her well?
qa.a: They might think she doesn't care about her Nani, when the flat facts are really a way of holding the pain back for now.

grounding: A teenager whose Nani has died talks about kidney failure in a flat quiz voice in the school library, and her grief surfaces only later at the gate.

I'm Jatin, Ramesh's cousin. I came to Bareilly for our Dadi's thirteenth-day prayers, and all week Ramesh was the calmest person in the house.
Whenever a relative arrived, he explained it like a news report. "Her heart stopped at 4:10 a.m. The doctor said it was a cardiac arrest, not a heart attack; they're different things. They tried for twenty-five minutes." He even corrected Bua when she mixed up the names of Dadi's tablets. His voice stayed flat, as if he were reading from a page.
The aunties whispered that he was very mature. I wasn't sure. He was sixteen, and Dadi had packed his tiffin every single school day of his life.
On the last night I went up to the terrace and found him sitting beside her folded shawl, shoulders shaking. I sat down next to him and didn't say anything.

qa.a: On the terrace, sitting beside Dadi's folded shawl, shoulders shaking.

qa.a: Jatin sat beside Ramesh without saying anything, giving the tears room instead of praising the calm or asking more questions.
